summary: Spyglass's 1950 lookout tower collapsed and was removed in 2014; the separate 1943 ground house was restored by 2019 and is now the rental.

facts.status_note: The 1950 53-ft tower's L-4 cab partially collapsed in July 2014 and was removed in an emergency operation; only the tower support structure remains. The separate ground house (moved to the site in 1943) survives and was fully restored in 2019.

access.note: Ground house available via Forest Service recreation rental program (recreation.gov); combination lock for gate and cabin.

visit.trail_note: Rental ground house, not the historic tower structure, which is a ruin and should not be climbed.

events.note: First used as a fire patrol point.
20-ft platform tower, log cabin, and barn erected.
50-ft pole tower with 7x7-ft cab replaced the 1922 tower.
Gable-roof L-4 cabin moved from McDonald Peak to serve as ground living quarters; later used for storage.
53-ft treated-timber tower with standard 1936-model L-4 cab built; this is the structure most commonly pictured.
Last staffed year, on emergency-staffed status.
Restoration work began on the ground cabin; tower left as a standing ruin.
Tower cab partially collapsed in July 2014, necessitating emergency removal.
Ground house restoration completed; opened as recreation rental.

evidence.supports: 1922 platform tower/barn, 1930 pole tower, 1950 53-ft tower w/ L-4 cab, last staffed 1978
evidence.quote: The present standard 53' CT-2 treated timber tower with standard 1936-model L-4 cab, built in 1950, was last staffed in 1978.

evidence.supports: 1943 L-4 cab moved for quarters, 2012 restoration start, 2014 tower collapse/removal
evidence.quote: In July 2014, the tower cab partially collapsed, necessitating its emergency removal. The ground cab has been fully restored and is available on the Recreation Rental program.

evidence.supports: 1911 patrol point reference confirmed on idahofirelookouts, staff list, 1978 emergency status, 2014 removal, 2019 renovation
evidence.quote:
1978 – Lookout was put on Emergency Staffed status.
The L-4 cabin was removed in 2014, but the support structure remains. Spyglass Ground house was renovated in 2019 and is currently on the Rental Program.

evidence.supports: 1911 patrol point start, operational to late 1960s, restoration 2012-2019, CCC outhouse, rental details
evidence.quote: It was first used as a patrol point in 1911 and by the 1920s supported a tower and housing for forest fire lookouts. It was an operational lookout until the mid- to late 60s and then abandoned in the 1970s... Extensive restoration of the ground house for use as a recreation rental cabin began in 2012 and was completed in 2019.

corrections.proposed: partially_removed / tower is a ruin, ground house is the standing rental
corrections.why: The brief's 'tower' kind/status implies the 53-ft L-4 tower is intact, but recreation.gov and firelookout.com confirm the tower cab collapsed and was removed in 2014; only the support structure remains. The rentable, restored structure is the separate 1943 ground house.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR/firelookout.com say 53-ft tower; idahofirelookouts.com says 41-ft TT L-4 tower. Story uses the 53-ft figure as it is corroborated by two sources including recreation.gov.

notes_for_editor: Brief lists kind=tower/status=standing, but the historic 53-ft L-4 tower cab collapsed and was removed in 2014 (see correction). What's rentable today is the separate restored ground house. Design field left as L-4 since both the (removed) tower cab and the (standing) ground house were L-4 type; editor may want a status field update to reflect the tower/groundhouse distinction. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04): draft named 'Robert and Wayne McCormick's families' as 1951 staff, but neither firelookout.com nor idahofirelookouts.com lists a Robert McCormick -- only Wayne McCormick (1951) is documented -- fixed to remove the fabricated name. Also rewrote the 1950-tower sentence, which closely echoed NHLR's own wording ('53' CT-2 treated timber tower with standard 1936-model L-4 cab'), into the story's own phrasing.
